title: The Fundamental Question of Edtech
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer reproduces a five-minute pitch to Gates Foundation leadership built on one question every edtech product answers implicitly: what are the humans good for and what is the tech good for. He characterizes the dominant Khan Academy style answer, in which software evaluates answers instantly, teachers are backup and other students are inhibitors, and cites Gates research that personalized learning schools show diminished belonging and safety. He contrasts a centaur model in his Amplify math curriculum, where the computer elicits and collects early student thinking and the teacher builds on it. The piece belongs in Ed-Tech because the role of the tool in the classroom is itself the subject under evaluation.
points: Every edtech product answers what the humans and the tech are each good for, even though that question is rarely asked aloud.
The dominant personalized-learning model makes teachers backup and students nearly irrelevant, and Gates research links it to lower belonging and safety.
In the centaur model the computer is a partner that elicits, collects and connects student and teacher thinking rather than grading it right or wrong.
Giving teachers a real-time view of early student work lets them turn a surprising response into a whole-class conversation.
The two models teach students very different ideas about mathematics and about themselves as math learners.
quotes: There is a fundamental question in edtech, one that’s rarely asked out loud even though every edtech company has an answer. What are the humans good for and what is the tech good for? And by humans I mean both the teachers and students.
What are teachers good for? The teachers are good for backup. They come along to fill in whatever needs the computer can’t meet.

What are the students good for? The answer, almost explicitly in these models, is “not much.” This edtech model sees other students as inhibitors of your learning, which is why they call it “personalized learning” rather than “socialized learning.

The costs of this model are becoming more broadly understood. For example, the Gates Foundation has been studying personalized learning nationwide since 2015 and has found that students in personalized learning schools feel diminished feelings of belonging and safety than students in the comparison group.

We don’t evaluate it as right or wrong because early student thinking is always a mix of both. Instead, we interpret student thinking back into the context. Here is the cannon person you meant to graph and here is the cannon person you graphed.

These two answers to the fundamental question of edtech can complement one another to a limited degree but they have many more differences than similarities. And those differences result in students learning very different ideas about mathematics and about themselves and their classmates as math learners.
